To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) extreme rejuvenation of bulk metallic glass (BMG) is possible by imposing large plastic deformation in compression; (ii) the rejuvenation is equivalent to the effect of quenching at ~1010 K s-1, which is many orders of magnitude higher than the quenching rate for BMG; (iii) the rejuvenation occurs in a large volume fraction of the material; (iv) the rejuvenation can be reversed by unloading, and (v)
extreme rejuvenation of bulk metallic glasses can be achieved by imposing plastic deformation in compression.
extreme rejuvenation of bulk metallic glass (Zr-based BMG) can be obtained by applying a compressive force in the absence of a shear band.

the deformation and failure mechanisms of bulk metallic glasses.
the deformation and mechanical properties of metallic glasses.
understanding the mechanisms of plasticity of metallic glasses, and the role of shear bands.

extreme plastic deformation can rejuvenate a bulk metallic glass to an extremely high-energy state that is equivalent to that of a liquid quenched at a cooling rate of ~10(10) K/s, which is many orders of magnitude greater than the fastest cooling rates that can be achieved in bulk samples.
extreme rejuvenation of metallic glasses is possible, but only in bulk if the deformation is constrained.

we have demonstrated that a metallic glass can be rejuvenated to a state that is equivalent to that obtain by quenching a liquid at a rate of ~1010 K s-1, a rate that is many orders of magnitude higher than that which is possible in bulk samples.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is now possible to rejuvenate a bulk metallic glass to the same extent that was previously possible only for shear bands.

the degree of rejuvenation that we have observed in the bulk of the glass is comparable to that obtained in the shear bands in previous work, and is equivalent to that obtained by quenching a liquid at a rate of ~1010  K s−1.

the plastic deformation in a bulk glass can be used to achieve an extreme state of rejuvenation, which would otherwise be possible only by quenching at a rate of 1010 K s–1, which is orders of magnitude faster.
